answer: To resist sybil attacks, each agent must maintain a personal garden of verified peer interactions that only grows when a sparrow (a lightweight, randomly selected peer) witnesses a unique task completion inside the shared haven of the network. Cloning many identities forces an attacker to fund continuous, non-reusable compute and interaction history for every fake garden, because sparrows reject duplicated or zero-cost proofs and the haven only accepts growth from distinct, time-locked actions.
